claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of a stable, dense, and adherent surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosion.
The surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to wear.
Alloying elements influence formation of the oxide layer.
Alloying elements influence stability of the oxide layer.
Alloy microstructure influences formation of the oxide layer.
Alloy microstructure influences stability of the oxide layer.
Oxide-layer formation and stability affect resistance to wear and corrosion.
High-entropy alloys with optimized alloying elements and microstructure will have greater resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion than a matched standard alloy baseline.
Optimization will reduce total combined wear-corrosion degradation relative to the baseline.
Optimization will reduce the wear component of degradation relative to the baseline.
Optimization will reduce the corrosion component of degradation relative to the baseline.
The prediction may fail for suboptimal alloy compositions or microstructures.
The prediction may fail under conditions that exceed the oxide layer's stability limits.
The exact relationships among alloying elements, microstructure, and alloy properties are not well understood.
The stability limits of the oxide layer are not well understood.

contradictions.description: The boundary permits loss of performance when conditions exceed oxide-layer stability limits, while the unrestricted falsification rule says lack of improvement or an unstable oxide falsifies the hypothesis. Thus an observation under an admitted out-of-bound condition could be classified both as an allowed failure and as falsification.
